chapters.title: Chapter 4: Choosing the Right ITR Form

lessons.title: ITR-1 to ITR-4: Which Form Fits Your Income

body.text: Your ITR form is decided by your most complicated income, not your biggest. ₹40 lakh of salary fits in ITR-1. A single Nifty options trade pushes the same person into ITR-3.

markDefs.definition: A return the department treats as incomplete or inconsistent, for example one filed on the wrong form. You are given a window, usually 15 days from the intimation, to fix it, failing which the return is treated as never filed.

children.text: The department notifies different ITR forms for different kinds of taxpayers, and each form has only the schedules its users need. File on a form that cannot hold all your income, and the department can treat it as a
under Section 139(9) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Picking the right form is the first real decision of filing day, and for individuals it comes down to four choices.

body.caption: The Four Individual ITR Forms for FY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27)

cells: ITR-1 (Sahaj)
Resident individuals
Salary or pension, up to two house properties, other sources like interest and dividends
Total income up to ₹50 lakh; long-term equity gains under Section 112A up to ₹1.25 lakh; agricultural income up to ₹5,000
ITR-2
Individuals and HUFs, resident or not
Everything in ITR-1, plus any capital gains, more house properties, foreign assets and income
No income cap; no business or professional income
ITR-3
Individuals and HUFs with business or professional income
Everything in ITR-2, plus business or profession, including F&O and intraday trading
No cap; the catch-all form for individuals
ITR-4 (Sugam)
Resident individuals, HUFs and firms other than LLPs
Presumptive business or professional income, plus salary, house property and other sources
Total income up to ₹50 lakh; Section 112A gains up to ₹1.25 lakh; no other capital gains

stats.label: ITR-3 and ITR-4, No Audit
stats.context: Separate date introduced by the Finance Act, 2026

children.text: ITR-1: The Simplest Form, With the Most Tripwires

ITR-1 is built for the typical salaried resident, and it got more flexible for AY 2026-27: it now accepts up to two house properties, and it continues to allow small long-term equity gains. But it has a long list of conditions, and breaking any one of them means you cannot use it. The next lesson walks through ITR-1 in detail. For now, learn the tripwires.

body.title: ITR-1: What Fits and What Forces You Out

columns.label: Fits in ITR-1
points: Salary from one or more employers, or pension
One self-occupied home and one let-out flat
Interest from savings accounts, FDs and bonds; dividends
Long-term gains on listed equity or equity funds up to ₹1.25 lakh, with no losses to carry forward
Family pension, and agricultural income up to ₹5,000

columns.label: Forces You to Another Form
points: Total income above ₹50 lakh, or being a non-resident
Any short-term capital gain, or long-term gains above ₹1.25 lakh
Being a director in a company, or holding unlisted equity shares during the year
Foreign assets, foreign income or signing authority in a foreign account
Brought-forward or carried-forward losses, business income, more than two house properties, or TDS on cash withdrawals under Section 194N

body.title: One Small Detail
body.question: Deepika earns a salary of ₹14,00,000 in Hyderabad, owns one let-out flat, and has a ₹60,000 long-term gain on an equity mutual fund. She also has a short-term capital loss of ₹30,000 from FY 2023-24 that she is still carrying forward. Which form should she file?
body.explanation: Everything about Deepika fits ITR-1 except the carried-forward capital loss. ITR-1 cannot hold brought-forward or carried-forward losses, and it allows Section 112A gains only when there are no such losses. To set off or keep carrying that loss forward, she needs ITR-2. Filing ITR-1 would also mean losing the loss.

children.text: ITR-2: For Investors, NRIs and Anyone Beyond ITR-1

If you have no business or professional income but fail any ITR-1 condition, ITR-2 is your form. It is the natural home for the Zerodha or Groww investor who booked short-term gains, the mutual fund investor with long-term gains above ₹1.25 lakh, the employee holding US stocks or RSUs, the director of a family company, the owner of three flats, anyone earning over ₹50 lakh, crypto investors reporting gains on virtual digital assets, and non-residents with income in India.

body.title: The NRI's Form
body.textWithBlank: Rahul lives in Dubai and qualifies as a non-resident for FY 2025-26. His only Indian income is rent from a flat in Pune and interest on his NRO account. He should file ITR-___.
body.explanation: ITR-1 and ITR-4 are only for residents, and Rahul has no business income, so ITR-2 is the right form. Being an NRI alone takes you out of ITR-1, however small your Indian income.

children.text: ITR-3 is for individuals and HUFs with income from a business or profession that they report on actual profit rather than on a presumptive basis, and for those who do not qualify for ITR-4. It covers freelancers and consultants who maintain books, partners in a firm, and above all traders: futures and options trading is non-speculative business income and intraday equity trading is speculative business income, so a salaried person who trades F&O files ITR-3 even if the trading result is a loss. ITR-3 can hold every other type of income too, so nobody is ever too complex for it.

body.text: Traders often ask whether they can skip F&O in their return because they lost money. Don't. The trades are reported to the department through your broker and the exchanges, so a return without them is an easy mismatch. More importantly, reporting an F&O loss in ITR-3 by the due date is the only way to carry it forward for 8 years and set it off against future business income.

children.text: ITR-4, called Sugam, is the business equivalent of ITR-1. It suits a resident doctor, lawyer, architect, designer or consultant declaring at least 50% of receipts as income under the presumptive scheme, a small trader declaring 6% or 8% of turnover, or a transporter under the goods carriage scheme. Total income must be within ₹50 lakh. It shares ITR-1's major restrictions: no directorships, no unlisted shares, no foreign assets, no losses to carry forward, and no capital gains beyond Section 112A gains up to ₹1.25 lakh.

cards.term: Salaried in Bengaluru, FD interest, ₹80,000 long-term gain on equity funds, no losses
cards.definition: ITR-1. The long-term gain is within ₹1.25 lakh and there are no losses to carry.

cards.term: The same person, plus a ₹20,000 short-term gain on shares
cards.definition: ITR-2. ITR-1 cannot hold any short-term capital gain.

cards.term: Salaried, owns three flats: one self-occupied, two let out
cards.definition: ITR-2. ITR-1 now allows two house properties, not three.

cards.term: Employee of a US tech company in Hyderabad holding vested RSUs
cards.definition: ITR-2. Foreign assets must go in Schedule FA, which ITR-1 does not have.

cards.term: Salaried, and a non-executive director on the board of the family's private company
cards.definition: ITR-2. Being a director in any company rules out ITR-1.

cards.term: Salaried techie who trades Nifty options on weekends
cards.definition: ITR-3. F&O is business income, even if it is a sideline and even if it made a loss.

cards.term: Dentist in Kochi, ₹30 lakh receipts, declares 50% under the presumptive scheme, nothing else
cards.definition: ITR-4. Presumptive professional income with total income within ₹50 lakh.

cards.term: Freelance designer on the presumptive scheme who also booked a short-term gain on shares
cards.definition: ITR-3. ITR-4 cannot hold short-term capital gains, so the catch-all form applies.

cards.term: Retired teacher with pension, bank interest and a profit on selling crypto
cards.definition: ITR-2. Gains on virtual digital assets are reported in a schedule ITR-1 does not have.

body.title: Fixing a Wrong Form
body.prompt: Mohit filed ITR-1 even though he had short-term capital gains. The department sends him an intimation that his return is defective. Within how many days of the intimation must he usually respond by filing a corrected return?
body.explanation: The usual window is 15 days from the date of the intimation. If he does nothing, the return is treated as if it was never filed, with the consequences of a missed return: no refund processing, possible late fees and lost carry-forward benefits. The corrected return must be on the right form, here ITR-2.

body.title: Four Forms Under One Roof
body.scenario: The Menon family lives in Kochi. Suresh, 52, works at a public sector bank, earns a salary of ₹24,00,000, lives in his own house, has FD interest and a ₹1,10,000 long-term gain on equity mutual funds, and no carried-forward losses. His wife Priya, 48, a dentist, has clinic receipts of ₹42,00,000 and declares 50% as income under the presumptive scheme; she also sold listed shares she had held for eight months. Their son Arjun, 24, is a software engineer in Pune earning ₹9,00,000 and trades weekly options on Groww. Suresh's mother Ammini, 78, gets a pension of ₹4,80,000 from her late husband's former employer, which she draws as family pension, along with ₹60,000 of interest from a bank other than the one crediting her pension.
body.prompt: Which ITR form does each family member file, and what is the deciding factor in each case?
body.modelAnswer: Suresh files ITR-1. He is resident, his income is within ₹50 lakh, and his long-term equity gain of ₹1,10,000 is within the ₹1.25 lakh that ITR-1 allows, with no losses to carry forward. Priya would have fitted ITR-4 on her presumptive professional income alone, and her total income of about ₹21 lakh is within the limit. But she has a short-term gain on shares, which ITR-4 cannot hold, so she files ITR-3. Arjun files ITR-3 because F&O trading is business income, regardless of his salary or whether the trades made money. Ammini's family pension is income from other sources. Her income of ₹5,40,000 comes to ₹5,15,000 after the ₹25,000 family pension deduction in the new regime, which is still above the basic exemption limit, so she must file. Because her interest comes from a different bank, the 75-and-above filing exemption does not apply, and she files ITR-1: resident, within ₹50 lakh, and only family pension and interest.

body.title: The other ITR forms, for completeness

content.caption: Forms You Will Rarely Need as an Individual

cells: ITR-5
Firms, LLPs, associations of persons and bodies of individuals
ITR-6
Companies, other than those claiming exemption as charitable institutions
ITR-7
Trusts, political parties, research institutions and others filing under specific exemption provisions
ITR-U
An updated return, used to report income left out of an earlier return and pay additional tax. Chapter 6 covers it.

body.title: Choose Your Form Before You Log In
steps: Confirm your residential status for FY 2025-26: resident or non-resident
Add up your total income and check whether it is above ₹50 lakh
Check for any F&O, intraday, freelance or other business or professional income
Check your broker and mutual fund statements for short-term gains or long-term gains above ₹1.25 lakh
Check for foreign assets, directorships, unlisted shares and carried-forward losses
Pick your form using the four-question path, and note its due date: 31 July for ITR-1 and ITR-2, 31 August for non-audit ITR-3 and ITR-4

points: The right form depends on your most complex income source, and filing the wrong one can make your return defective, usually with 15 days to fix it
ITR-1 suits resident individuals with income up to ₹50 lakh from salary, up to two house properties, other sources and Section 112A gains up to ₹1.25 lakh
Short-term gains, larger long-term gains, foreign assets, directorships, unlisted shares, carried-forward losses or NRI status all move you to ITR-2
Any business or professional income, including F&O and intraday trading, means ITR-3, unless it is purely presumptive and fits ITR-4
ITR-4 is for residents with presumptive income and total income up to ₹50 lakh, with the same major restrictions as ITR-1
For FY 2025-26, ITR-1 and ITR-2 are due on 31 July 2026, and non-audit ITR-3 and ITR-4 on 31 August 2026

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax advice. Eligibility conditions for each ITR form are notified every year and change often. The position described reflects the forms notified for AY 2026-27 at the time of writing. Always read the instructions for the current year's forms on the Income Tax Department's portal, or consult a qualified tax professional.
